“Friendslop” is a term that has been becoming increasingly popular lately, and I feel like it diminishes something very valuable: a game that makes you laugh with your friends. A game like R.E.P.O.

In R.E.P.O., we have to collect a series of objects, fit them into a small, limited-space cart, bring them back to the base, and sell them for enough money to advance to the next level. The more objects we put in the cart, the less space we have, and questions start to arise: Will this object fit? Could I make it work if I rearrange everything? Will I be able to move the cart without everything falling out?

Now add the fact that every object has its own size, shape, durability, weight, and behavior. And, to add even more tension, there are monsters capable not only of killing us, but also of destroying what we are carrying in the cart. Each one has its own unique way of interacting with us and our environment.

As we progress through the game and heavier objects start appearing, we are (almsot always) forced to work with someone else to carry them and figure out how to get them back to the base. It is similar to moving houses, where a couple of people have to figure out how to carry and fit some enormous piece of furniture through a tiny doorway. Except here, you cannot just sit down and think about it or stand still for too long, because you might get hit with a jumpscare that makes you drop the object, break it, or simply die.

With all these variables, it is no surprise that R.E.P.O. has become the clip-generating machine that it was—and still is. But these moments are not simply the result of putting realistic physics into a game and waiting for something funny to happen. They are the result of good design.

And even its premise fits into this. The “story” is basically about a greedy tax collector who sends us out to repossess things, while we carry out the job as the result of an “apparent debt.” It is about greed and ambition.

And believe me: many times you will find yourself wondering whether what you are carrying in that cart is really worth it. Whether it is worth risking everything for one more valuable object, even when you already have enough to finish the level.

(Spoiler: greed comes at a cost.)

R.E.P.O. is not particularly visually creative, it does not have a deep or terrifying story, and it does not even have an ending. . And it does not need any of that to convey a feeling. All it needs is its own language: physics, order, and strategy in an arcade game, with money essentially functioning as the score.

The language of video games.

R.E.P.O definitely jumped onto the Lethal Company hype train, and somehow managed to. in some areas, do it even better.

The biggest difference is the physics. Loot actually loses value if you smash it around, so suddenly carrying a television through a doorway becomes a high-stakes engineering operation. It adds a simple extra layer of challenge that creates a lot of very stupid, very funny situations.

The creatures also fit the game perfectly. They're comically creepy (and weirdly cute) thanks to the art style. I still think Lethal Company has the edge when it comes to creative enemy AI behavior, but R.E.P.O's monsters are still great. Absolutely a must-play with friends.

9/10

There are some issues with the game that i currently have:

How valuables are damaged or break. Specifically, i find it that valuables can be damaged way too easily or take more damage then it should. An example is with the Dino Skeleton, dragging it on the floor while holding up the front of it, it got damaged and lost a lot of value. In another case.

The physics: I lost an entire money bag by having it bounce off the floor and into the void. I do admit that it may partially be my fault since there was no cart under it since i didnt want to cross the wooden plank but simply put valuables on the extract, but losing that entire money bag was quite annoying.

Monsters: Some of them seem to easily get clipped or glitched in some way. An example was when the Clown was glitched and couldnt move, and was stuck on a loop kicking the cart while doing no damage to the valuables. In order to fix the situation, i had to move the cart, which resulted in my character dying. I dont know if this is because it genuinely was glitched and couldnt move, or it insisted on following a specific path that was blocked.

Cosmetics: Currently i am trying to collect as many cosmetics as i can since i do enjoy the customization options for it, but there are way too many green boxes, especially in the levels where cosmetic boxes have a higher chance to be blue or even purple. I have gone through dryspells of only green boxes from extract 6 to extract 9 (where i mainly farm them). Yellow boxes appear extremely rarely (I believe to have found only 5).

Considering that this game is still in early access, even with the small issues mentioned, i still believe that it is a great game and fun to play, especially when on discount. It also runs quite well on older hardware
